episode_thesis: Katie Kaminski argues, from her paper 'Trade War: Crisis or Correction?', that trend following usually loses in the first phase of an equity drawdown below about 15% because shocks run against prevailing trends, and earns crisis alpha (second-responder payoff) only in deeper or longer drawdowns, so April 2025 is either a short dislocation like 2018/2020 or the start of something like the tech bubble. Wide dispersion across trend managers in a shock is normal (position placement, parameters and speed, like coin tosses), robust managers diversify parameters, and adding trend to equities turns the question into a joint portfolio-construction and risk problem (correlation and volatility handling). Niels Kaastrup-Larsen adds the April 2025 performance numbers, the long-gold crowding survey and the point that drawdown periods are historically when to allocate.

speakers.name: Katie Kaminski
speakers.role: trend-following researcher (guest co-host); author of the paper 'Trade War: Crisis or Correction? Managed futures and crisis alpha in 2025'
speakers.speaker_note: Recorded Thursday morning mid-April 2025 (data as of Tuesday 15 April; uploaded 2025-04-25). Captions garble names (Makita is a consultant framework name as captioned; Ying Shan, Tyler Lovingood). Some turns inside C03 and C13 run together between speakers; attribution follows the ledger.

worldview_premises.premise: Shocks usually run against prevailing trends, so trend followers are often on the wrong side initially; what they earn depends on where they stood before the shock and how fast the system adjusts to the new trend.
worldview_premises.support: her drawdown study across S&P peak-to-trough episodes by depth and duration; first-hand experience of shocks

worldview_premises.premise: Crisis alpha is a search, not a guarantee: different crises need different tools (first, second and third responders), so build a portfolio with attributes that catch different phases. Trend is a second responder.
worldview_premises.support: her original 'In Search of Crisis Alpha' work; consultant framework

worldview_premises.premise: Return dispersion across trend managers in extreme shocks is normal and largely luck of positioning, like coin tosses; small differences in position size, direction or parameters produce big return differences.
worldview_premises.support: Andrew Lo penny-toss classroom experiment analogy; her papers on return dispersion; 2022 bond trend example

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following should be market-agnostic: markets dismissed for decades (precious and industrial metals, cocoa) trended when macro conditions changed, so the signal should decide when to trade; there is no magic speed and speed tilts by asset class have little statistical evidence.
worldview_premises.support: historical episodes (metals, cocoa, soybeans in April 2025); lack of statistical evidence for speed tilts

worldview_premises.premise: The trend industry has moved to slower systems for cost and to harvest long-term risk premia; that lowers diversification (trend looks like equities) and makes pivoting in dislocations harder, so some reactivity helps.
worldview_premises.support: her speed decomposition of the index

worldview_premises.premise: Stocks and bonds are positively correlated when inflation or rates drive them, so being long both is more risk, but correlations are volatile and must be measured and managed skeptically; a risk model with a long-term negative stock-bond correlation underestimates risk.
worldview_premises.support: April 2025 flip in correlation of US assets with equities; her 'bonds behaving badly' paper

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility tells the range, not the direction: even perfect foresight of volatility barely improves trend performance, so volatility is mainly about balancing risk and signal-to-noise.
worldview_premises.support: an internal analysis with a researcher assuming perfect volatility prediction

mechanism_chains.topic: Why trend loses early in an equity drawdown and wins only if the drawdown deepens or lengthens

steps.from: A sudden shock hits against existing trend positions (long equities)
steps.to: Trend losses in the first part of the drawdown (typically drawdowns under about 15%)
steps.why: positions are on the wrong side and must adjust to the new theme

steps.from: The drawdown becomes deeper and longer (tech bubble, GFC, 2022)
steps.to: Trend turns positive: crisis alpha as a second responder
steps.why: the system has repositioned and rides the unravelling in the slipstream of the selloff

steps.from: A short, sharp drawdown that recovers (2018, 2020)
steps.to: Trend stays weak, as in early 2025
steps.why: the shock reverses before trend can adjust

mechanism_chains.evidence: Bubble chart of managed futures returns by S&P drawdown depth and length; split of deep episodes into short sharp recoveries versus extended crises; S&P fell 18.7% (19 Feb to 8 Apr 2025) while SG CTA fell 8.6% and SG Trend 10.76%.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Few data points exist above 15% drawdown, so the second-responder claim rests on a handful of episodes; 2025 so far (20-30 days) is too short to tell whether it resembles the tech bubble start (500+ days).

mechanism_chains.topic: Why April 2025 differed from the usual risk-off pattern

steps.to: Yields rose and the dollar fell instead of bonds and the dollar rallying
steps.why: vulnerability in US assets and foreign selling; tariffs also threaten inflation

steps.from: Bonds and dollar fail as havens
steps.to: Fixed income offered no offset to the equity and currency losses of trend; JGBs added a short squeeze
steps.why: trend positions assumed the usual hedge behaviour

steps.to: Trend over longer horizons can capture the seismic shift as new trends emerge
steps.why: trend follows persistent macro trends, not free fall

mechanism_chains.evidence: Market moves in April 2025; trend indices year to date.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: If the regime shift reverses quickly (a policy reversal) trend positions would be wrong again; she does not say this explicitly but calls the situation unpredictable.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why stacking trend on equities is a new optimisation problem

steps.from: Futures margin lets trend be added on top of an equity holding (150-200% exposure without more capital)
steps.to: A combined objective: joint risk, rebalancing and holdability instead of standalone best Sharpe
steps.why: trend is not independent of equities; if trend is fully long equities the combination doubles equity exposure

steps.from: Rebalancing between equities and trend over time
steps.to: Return from the relationship and a more holdable portfolio
steps.why: investors judge each sleeve 'what have you done for me lately'

mechanism_chains.evidence: Reference to the 'Taming the Skew' paper and her own research; no numbers given.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Naive stacking ('classic portable alpha') ignores the shared equity exposure.

decision_process.practice: In a drawdown rerun the existing analysis code on the data (depth and duration of S&P drawdowns versus past episodes) instead of reacting; on multi-sigma days follow the process.
decision_process.why: emotions push for action on extreme days; history provides perspective (1% S&P move is about one sigma)

decision_process.practice: Aggregate several trend measures and adjust for changing volatility; avoid very simple single-parameter implementations; diversify parameters and methods.
decision_process.why: simple parameters create more return dispersion (the 100-day versus 105-day example)

decision_process.practice: Stay agnostic across all markets and let the signal decide when to trade; do not drop markets that looked poor in backtests.
decision_process.why: metals, cocoa and others trended after decades of apparent uselessness

decision_process.practice: Keep trend speeds mixed with some reactivity; tilt speed by asset class only marginally and only to the level of statistical evidence.
decision_process.why: slow-only systems cannot pivot in dislocations, while long-term-premium systems look like equities; evidence for speed specialisation is slim

decision_process.practice: Size positions by volatility so risk is balanced across assets (10% vol currencies versus 40% vol commodities means 4:1), like risk parity; volatility also enters signal strength as signal-to-noise.
decision_process.why: balances risk across assets; but in 2022 bond volatility doubling forced a rethink of risk per asset

decision_process.practice: Incorporate correlations into the risk model (stock-bond correlation sign matters) while staying skeptical of their volatility; decide how much to include shocks and jumps in volatility estimates (nickel event).
decision_process.why: correlation says where the risk is; a negative-correlation assumption understates risk when it turns positive

decision_process.practice: When combining equities and trend, risk-manage the two jointly and rebalance rather than stacking naively.

speakers.evidence_style: Empirical studies of her own (drawdown bubble charts, return-dispersion papers, speed decomposition, perfect-volatility test) plus analogies (coin tosses, cliff positions) and long history ('800 years' dataset mentioned); uses pictures to gain emotional perspective.

current_views.view: The tariff shock moved markets into a new regime in which equities fell while yields rose and the dollar fell, signalling vulnerability in US assets; the rest of the year could be interesting as new themes emerge.
current_views.reasoning: unusual safe-haven behaviour in bonds and the dollar; tariff-driven inflation threat; foreign selling of US assets

current_views.view: The 2025 episode so far (20-30 days) looks like the start of the tech bubble drawdown; if recession or inflation develops this is only the beginning of the story.
current_views.reasoning: overlay of current drawdown on extended crisis paths in her paper

current_views.view: Bonds are hard to trade now: a huge curve steepener is possible even if short rates are cut, if foreign selling and tariff inflation persist.
current_views.reasoning: foreign selling of US assets plus tariff inflation

current_views.view: Bonds are still behaving badly; fixed income became vulnerable after 2020, so correlations matter more.
current_views.reasoning: inflation threat and risk to US assets

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: host of Top Traders Unplugged, veteran hedge fund manager and trend follower (about 40 years in markets)
speakers.speaker_note: Reads headlines and index numbers; argues positions on allocation timing, chaos versus crisis, dispersion and correlation use. Ledger correction applied: the Powell headline (C01) and the short-term traders index figure (C05) are his.

worldview_premises.premise: CTAs lose money in a shock because of how they were positioned before it, not because of the market move itself; after a painful CTA drawdown is historically when to allocate.
worldview_premises.support: history of CTA drawdowns and index drawdown data (SG indices versus S&P drawdowns)

worldview_premises.premise: Classification schemes give no guarantee (long Treasuries, a textbook first responder, failed in April 2025); there may be different kinds of shock (chaos versus crisis) needing different alpha solutions.
worldview_premises.support: April 2025 observation and personal feel ('could not back this up academically')

worldview_premises.premise: Differently designed trend models perform similarly in the long run, but in short or crisis periods the choice of speed, parameters and position sizing can create big differences.
worldview_premises.support: a half-remembered paper (100-day versus 105-day moving average about 20% difference in a year); replicator providers admitting luck

worldview_premises.premise: What differentiates one trend engine from another is trading speed, market universe and weights, and risk management; volatility scaling is the one common driver that makes managers trade at the same time.

Correlation cannot be measured reliably over short windows, so being too precise on correlations in a chaotic period may not help; some CTAs ignore correlation and rely on entries and stops, which still leaves them exposed but protected by stops.
worldview_premises.support: defence of correlation-free managers; no data

worldview_premises.premise: Removing markets from a universe after poor backtest results risks missing later trends (cocoa looked poor for about 15 years then trended).

decision_process.practice: Use return-stacking and portable alpha products to add trend to a full portfolio; keep tracking how good the trend engine is separately from the combined return stream.
decision_process.why: adding trend can improve upside and reduce downside, but a single combined stream hides the quality of the alpha engine, even though investors prefer one line item

decision_process.practice: Use Katie's drawdown study as a diagnostic by comparing the depth and duration of the current S&P drawdown with past episodes to judge short-term dislocation versus structural regime change.

speakers.evidence_style: Cites index data, survey headlines and charts from others, and personal experience of 40 years; openly flags recall as uncertain and views as feelings.

current_views.view: April 2025 trend losses came mostly from equities and currencies with no fixed-income offset; JGBs were a short squeeze; gold, energies and short-term rates were bright spots (not universal; Europe strongest). Mid-April YTD: BTOP50 -5.26%, SG CTA -8.36%, SG Trend -10.84%, short-term traders about -1%, versus S&P 500 TR -9.95%, MSCI World about -6.5%, US aggregate bonds +2%.
Removing Powell from the Fed would worsen the turmoil; Powell said tariffs were much bigger than expected, leaving the Fed on pause under its dual mandate.
current_views.reasoning: personal opinion; Powell's remarks at the Economic Club of Chicago

current_views.view: Long gold has replaced the Magnificent 7 as the most crowded trade in the Bank of America fund manager survey and CTAs are also long gold.
The shock feels like chaos more than crisis; the CTA drawdown is uncomfortable but historically the time to allocate. Some trend managers with 30-40 year records are in their worst-ever drawdown.
current_views.reasoning: personal sense and index drawdown history

disagreements.topic: Crisis versus chaos: do different shocks need different alpha?

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: April 2025 feels like chaos rather than crisis and may need a different alpha solution; a classic first responder (long Treasuries) failed.

positions.speaker: Katie Kaminski
positions.position: Crisis alpha is a search, not a guarantee; different crises need different tools, so build a portfolio with first/second/third-responder attributes; chaos alpha comes from volatility strategies or even cash.

disagreements.topic: Whether correlations belong in position sizing

positions.speaker: Katie Kaminski
positions.position: Correlation tells you where risk is and matters, especially since 2020 when stock-bond correlation turned positive; be skeptical of its volatility.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Some CTAs ignore correlation and use entries and stops, which still exposes them but protects with stops; precise correlation estimates are unreliable over short windows and may not help in chaotic periods.

positions.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
positions.position: Long run model type does not matter much, but in short or crisis periods speed, parameters and static versus dynamic sizing create big differences.

positions.speaker: Katie Kaminski
positions.position: Dispersion in shocks is mostly positioning luck and simple single-parameter systems; robust managers diversify parameters and methods.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The 15% threshold is read from a bubble chart and the paper has few observations above 15%, so conclusions about crisis alpha in deep drawdowns rest on a handful of episodes (tech bubble, GFC, 2022).

The 2025 drawdown (18.7% peak to trough) sits just below the 20% level where trend has typically turned positive, and trend had not turned by the low; whether it resolves as a short dislocation or an extended crisis is open.
Niels recalls a paper on 100-day versus 105-day moving averages with a roughly 20% performance gap but cannot name the source; the claim is unverified and he later says the numbers are illustrative.
Replicator providers 'admit they were lucky' is hearsay with no source.
Niels says crisis versus chaos is a feeling he cannot back academically; no evidence offered for different chaos alpha solutions.

The first part says trend 'tends to lose' under 15% drawdowns while the long-gold crowding and short-term-rate gains are bright spots; no breakdown by market is given for how much trend loss came from positioning versus signal lag.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Katie names the S&P drawdown depth and duration relative to past episodes (below or above about 15-20% and tens versus hundreds of days), whether recession or inflation develops, bond and dollar behaviour (steepener, safe-haven failure), stock-bond correlation sign, and a signal-driven policy trend. Horizon: months, since trend needs the drawdown to extend before it earns crisis alpha. Niels adds crowding (long gold most crowded) and CTA drawdown depth as signals for when to allocate.
reader_inferences: (reader) Both speakers frame April 2025 as a test of positioning (where trend stood before the shock), so the forward-looking question is whether trends in bonds, the dollar and gold persist; neither makes a price forecast.

(reader) Katie's 15% threshold implies that a trend allocation decision made during a sub-15% drawdown is mostly a decision about holding through the wrong-side phase, with the payoff arriving only if the drawdown deepens.
(reader) Niels's allocate-after-drawdown advice and Katie's second-responder story are consistent but untested here; no allocation timing statistics are given.
